intro_text:
Olympic Beach is the English rendering of Olympiaki Akti, a settlement of the Katerini municipality in Pieria, Central Macedonia, on Greece's Thermaic Gulf coast. It did not exist as an inhabited place until 1980. Until 1986 it was called Parathalassia Katerini — "Seaside Katerini" — before being renamed after Mount Olympus, whose summit, Mytikas, rises about 26 kilometers inland. Locals still sometimes call the area Katerinoskala, "Katerini's landing," the older name for a stretch of coast that has long served as the city's access point to the sea.

The 2021 census puts the population at either 236 residents, per the infobox on the English Wikipedia article, or 420, per the Greek article — the two disagree and neither cites a source that resolves it. Whatever the true figure, it is a fraction of the town's summer capacity: hotels, rental rooms, bungalows, and a campground line the shore and fill through July and August, then empty by October.

The beach sits about 7.5 kilometers from Katerini's center and roughly 3 kilometers south of Paralia, a larger neighbor with about 928 year-round residents, founded after 1922 by refugees from Cius in Asia Minor, and itself called Vromeroskala — "Foul Landing" — before its own rebrand. The pattern repeats along this coast: functional 20th-century boat landings, renamed for tourism.

The water is calm. Open-Meteo's ERA5 marine reanalysis for 2023–2024 puts the annual mean wave height at 0.35 meters, the biggest month, January, at 0.57 meters, and the calmest, June, at 0.2 meters; the largest modeled day reached 1.16 meters. The EU rates the bathing water "1 – excellent," and the beach has carried the Blue Flag every year except 1998, per the Greek Wikipedia article, though no available source explains that gap year.

Mount Olympus is not on this stretch of coast — it's visible on clear days, but the peak, Mytikas, at 2,917.7 meters, sits inland on the border of Thessaly and Macedonia. In myth it was the dwelling of the twelve Olympian gods; its first confirmed ascent came 2 August 1913, when guide Christos Kakkalos led Swiss climbers Frédéric Boissonnas and Daniel Baud-Bovy to the summit. Wikipedia's own disambiguation note for "Olympic Beach" has to distinguish this village from the beach venues of actual Olympic Games — a branding coincidence, not shared history.
spike_explainer:
Olympic Beach is a naming decision wearing a place. The settlement Wikipedia calls Olympiaki Akti did not exist until 1980, and it did not carry the name Olympic Beach until 1986. For six years before that it was Parathalassia Katerini, "Seaside Katerini," a plain descriptive label for a strip of Thermaic Gulf shoreline serving the inland city of Katerini, 7.5 kilometers away. Locals still sometimes use an older, more functional name for the same stretch of coast: Katerinoskala, "Katerini's landing." The city's own port authority station, the 3rd Port Authority Department of Skala Katerini, still sits here — a small piece of the working infrastructure the tourist name was built to obscure.

**What the rename bought.** Renaming Seaside Katerini to Olympiaki Akti in 1986 borrowed the prestige of Mount Olympus, Greece's highest mountain and, in myth, the dwelling of the twelve Olympian gods. It is a marketing move common enough along Greek beaches that the pattern is visible in the next settlement north. Paralia, three kilometers away and today the larger of the two towns with about 928 year-round residents, was founded after 1922 by refugees from Cius in Asia Minor and was originally named Vromeroskala — "Foul Landing." Its rebrand, dropping the unflattering "vromero" for the generic, pleasant "Paralia" ("beach"), predates Olympic Beach's own rename by decades and establishes the template: functional 20th-century boat landings, serving an inland farming town, renamed once tourism started to matter more than the landing did.

**The mountain the name borrows.** Mount Olympus itself is not on this beach, or even close to it in any way a swimmer would notice. Mytikas, the summit, stands 2,917.7 meters above sea level, about 26 kilometers to the southwest as the crow flies, at the boundary between Thessaly and Macedonia. In Greek myth it was the seat of the Olympian pantheon: Zeus, Hera, and the rest. In recorded history, the first confirmed ascent of the peak came on 2 August 1913, when the local guide Christos Kakkalos led the Swiss climbers Frédéric Boissonnas and Daniel Baud-Bovy to the top — a climb that happened 67 years before anyone lived permanently on the beach that now carries the mountain's name. The connection between the two places is visual and promotional, not geographic: on a clear day, swimmers can see the mountain's silhouette across the plain. That's the entire relationship.

**A name so generic it collides with itself.** The naming choice was not even original within its own encyclopedia entry. Wikipedia's English-language article for Olympiaki Akti carries a disambiguation notice pointing readers who searched "Olympic Beach" toward a different article entirely: the list of beach venues built for actual Olympic Games, the sand courts and seaside facilities constructed for Games like Athens 2004. A search engine, or a careless visitor, cannot immediately tell a small Greek resort village from Olympic Games infrastructure. That collision is a small, telling data point about how replaceable and interchangeable "Olympic" branding is when applied to real estate rather than reserved for the Games themselves.

**What's actually verifiable and what isn't.** The 1980 settlement date and the 1986 rename both come from the Greek-language Wikipedia article's specific wording — "κατοικήθηκε για πρώτη φορά το 1980" ("first inhabited in 1980") and "μέχρι το 1986 ονομαζόταν Παραθαλάσσια Κατερίνη" ("until 1986 was named Parathalassia Katerini") — sourced claims, not folklore, though Wikipedia itself is a tertiary source and the underlying municipal records are not linked from the article. The population figure is genuinely contested: the English infobox says 236 as of the 2021 census; the Greek article's body text says 420 for the same census year. Both cite "the 2021 census" without a linkable primary document, and this write-up cannot resolve the gap. What can be stated plainly is that whichever number is correct, it describes a small permanent population supporting a hotel-and-bungalow tourist economy that scales up substantially every summer and empties by autumn — the actual, unglamorous economic structure sitting underneath the mythological name.

**Why this matters for a beach page.** Most beach naming stories are either ancient (a place named for a saint or a shipwreck centuries ago) or corporate (a resort chain's brand). Olympic Beach is neither. It is a mid-1980s administrative rename of a functional coastal landing, timed to align with Greece's growing package-tourism economy, executed by a small municipality that had a genuinely dramatic mountain 26 kilometers away and decided that was close enough to trade on. The beach itself, its sand, its water quality, its calm winter surf, is unrelated to the decision. The name is doing marketing work the geography only partly supports, and the paper trail for that decision, thin as it is, survives in two disagreeing Wikipedia articles and a port authority office that still uses the older, more honest name.
honest_reckoning_note:
The uncomfortable fact about Olympic Beach is how little history is actually under the name. This is not a place that earned a mythological identity over centuries; it's a strip of coastal accommodation that existed for six years under the flatly descriptive name Seaside Katerini before a municipality swapped in Mount Olympus, a mountain 26 kilometers away, because that peak already carried international brand value. There was no archaeological find here, no royal visit, no ancient ruin on-site — just a 1986 rebrand of a beach-and-bungalow strip serving an inland farming town's day-trippers. Even Wikipedia can't settle the basic facts under the branding: its two language editions disagree by nearly 200 residents on the same 2021 census, and the disambiguation note admitting the name gets confused with Olympic Games beach-sport venues is itself a quiet admission of how generic the choice was.

None of this makes the beach a bad place to swim. Water quality is EU-rated excellent, the surf is genuinely gentle year-round, and the Blue Flag has flown here every year except 1998. What it means is that Olympic Beach does not have a deep relationship to Mount Olympus, to Greek myth, or to the Olympic Games. It is a small, calm stretch of the Thermaic Gulf that a 1986 municipal decision associated with the most famous mountain in the country, and that association has outlasted any scrutiny of whether it was ever earned.
reckoning_pullquote: A 1986 municipal rename, not myth or history, is why this beach carries the name of the most famous mountain in Greece.

margin_notes.text: The 3rd Port Authority Department of Skala Katerini (Λιμεναρχείο) still operates from Olympiaki Akti — the functioning remnant of the settlement's original job as Katerini's boat landing, before the beach identity existed.

A permanent population of a few hundred supporting hotels, rental rooms, bungalows, and a campground is a common ratio on the Pierian coast: infrastructure built for a summer population many times the year-round one.

Paralia's founders were part of the roughly 1.2 million ethnic Greeks resettled from Asia Minor after the 1922 population exchange following the Greco-Turkish War — the same wave that founded dozens of similarly named 'Nea' (New) towns across northern Greece.

The dataset's sand composition (50.9% quartz, 6.4% feldspar, 42.7% lithic fragments, described as a 'lithic-rich volcanic/collisional terrane') is a GloPrSM model prediction from satellite and geologic mapping, not a lab-tested sample taken on this beach.

A 0.35-meter annual mean wave height and a 1.16-meter peak modeled day are consistent with a semi-enclosed gulf: the Thermaic Gulf is sheltered from open Aegean swell by the Chalkidiki peninsula to the east.

The Wikipedia disambiguation for "Olympic Beach" routes searchers to the article on beach venues built for actual Olympic Games (such as beach volleyball courts) — an unrelated use of the same generic name.

day_in_time.dawn: The coast here faces roughly east into the Thermaic Gulf, so sunrise comes up directly over the water; per the wave data, the sea is at its calmest in June mornings, before any onshore breeze builds.
day_in_time.midday: Summer heat and haze usually blur out the Mount Olympus silhouette to the southwest; the beach itself, rated '1 – excellent' for bathing water, fills with the hotel and bungalow guests who make up most of its warm-weather population.
day_in_time.golden: Because the shoreline faces the gulf to the east, the beach does not get a sea sunset; instead, late light falls behind the town, over the inland ridgeline toward Mount Olympus, 26 kilometers off.
day_in_time.night: Outside July and August the settlement is quiet — a permanent population in the low hundreds, per the disputed 2021 census figures, in a town built to hold many times that many visitors.

food_drink.name: Waterfront tavernas
food_drink.description: Wikipedia's infobox-level description of Olympiaki Akti lists 'hotels, rental rooms, bungalows and camping facilities as well as restaurants' along the shore; expect grilled Thermaic Gulf fish and standard Greek taverna fare rather than a distinct local cuisine.

food_drink.name: Souvlaki and gyro stands
food_drink.description: Casual grilled-meat stands are standard along the coastal promenade and bike path that connects Olympiaki Akti to Paralia, geared to beach day-trippers rather than destination dining.

food_drink.name: Ouzo and tsipouro
food_drink.description: The standard aperitifs of northern Greek coastal dining, served with meze at the same waterfront tavernas; this write-up could not verify any specific bar or restaurant name for Olympic Beach itself, so none is listed here.

timeline.title: First confirmed ascent of Mount Olympus
timeline.description: Local guide Christos Kakkalos leads Swiss climbers Frédéric Boissonnas and Daniel Baud-Bovy to the summit of Mytikas on 2 August 1913 — 67 years before anyone lived permanently on the beach later named for the mountain.

timeline.title: Paralia founded by Asia Minor refugees
timeline.description: The neighboring town of Paralia, 3 km north, is founded after 1922 by refugees from Cius in Asia Minor, part of the post-war Greek population exchange; it was originally named Vromeroskala ("Foul Landing").

timeline.title: Olympic Beach first inhabited
timeline.description: The settlement is first inhabited in 1980 under the name Parathalassia Katerini ("Seaside Katerini"), a functional descriptor for Katerini's stretch of coast.

timeline.title: Joins the municipality of Katerini
timeline.description: The settlement becomes part of the municipality of Katerini, per Greek local-government records.
timeline.source: EETAA (Hellenic Agency for Local Development and Local Government), cited in Wikipedia: Olympiaki Akti

timeline.title: Renamed Olympiaki Akti
timeline.description: The settlement drops the descriptive name Parathalassia Katerini and is renamed Olympiaki Akti ("Olympic Beach" / "Olympic Coast"), trading on the fame of Mount Olympus, 26 km away.

timeline.title: The one year without the Blue Flag
timeline.description: Olympiaki Akti is awarded the EU Blue Flag every year except 1998; no source consulted for this page documents why that year broke the run.

timeline.title: Kallikratis reform reorganizes Paralia
timeline.description: Greece's Kallikratis local-government reform folds the neighboring, formerly independent municipality of Paralia into the municipality of Katerini as a municipal unit — the same administrative parent Olympiaki Akti had joined thirty years earlier.

timeline.title: "Silver Arrow" express train launched
timeline.description: An express electric train service named the Silver Arrow launches on 20 May 2019, running Athens–Thessaloniki with only two intermediate stops, Lianokladi and Larissa. It bypasses Katerini, whose station relies on the InterCity and Proastiakos services that feed the same upgraded trunk line.

timeline.title: 2021 census: population disputed between sources
timeline.description: The Greek census records the settlement's population, but the English and Greek Wikipedia articles report different figures for the same count — 236 and 420 respectively — without a shared, linkable source.

zones.name: Olympiaki Akti waterfront
zones.character: The main tourist strip: hotels, rental rooms, bungalows, and a campground along the sand, per Wikipedia's description of the settlement's tourist infrastructure.
zones.best_for: Swimming, sunbathing, the calmest average wave heights of the year in June
zones.notes: EU bathing water rating '1 – excellent' at monitoring site ELBW099047006101.

zones.name: Skala Katerini port authority station
zones.character: The functional anchor of the older name Katerinoskala: the 3rd Port Authority Department of Skala Katerini is based here, a working administrative office rather than a tourist draw.
zones.notes: Predates the 1986 tourist rebrand; still uses the older functional name.

zones.name: Coastal promenade toward Paralia
zones.character: A lit waterfront walkway and bike path connecting Olympiaki Akti to the larger neighboring resort of Paralia, about 3 km north.
zones.best_for: Walking, cycling between the two settlements
zones.notes: Paralia itself was renamed from Vromeroskala ("Foul Landing") after its 1922 founding.

zones.name: Agios Prokopios village center
zones.character: The settlement's inland core around its parish church, away from the beachfront hotels — the residential side of a place whose year-round population is disputed between 236 and 420.
zones.notes: Central church is Agios Prokopios (Saint Prokopios).

landmarks.name: Agios Prokopios Church
landmarks.description: The central parish church of Olympiaki Akti, dedicated to Saint Prokopios, whose feast day (8 July in the Orthodox calendar) is the settlement's nearest thing to a fixed local festival.

landmarks.name: Mount Olympus
landmarks.description: Greece's highest mountain (Mytikas, 2,917.7 m), about 26 km southwest of the beach in a straight line, visible from the shore on clear days and the source of the settlement's 1986 rename.

landmarks.name: 3rd Port Authority Department of Skala Katerini
landmarks.description: A functioning Hellenic Coast Guard / port authority office at Olympiaki Akti, the administrative remnant of the settlement's original role as Katerini's coastal landing.

cultural_refs.title: Mount Olympus in Greek mythology
cultural_refs.description: In Greek myth, Olympus was the dwelling of the twelve Olympian gods, including Zeus and Hera; the beach's 1986 name trades on that association despite sitting 26 km from the mountain.

cultural_refs.title: First ascent of Mount Olympus (1913)
cultural_refs.creator: Christos Kakkalos, Frédéric Boissonnas, Daniel Baud-Bovy
cultural_refs.description: The mountain's first confirmed ascent, on 2 August 1913, predates permanent habitation of the beach later named for it by 67 years.

cultural_refs.title: Naming collision with Olympic Games beach venues
cultural_refs.description: Wikipedia's English article on Olympiaki Akti carries a disambiguation note distinguishing the village from the unrelated list of beach venues built for actual Olympic Games.

cultural_refs.title: Paralia's 1922 refugee founding
cultural_refs.description: The neighboring resort of Paralia was founded by refugees from Cius, Asia Minor, part of the post-Greco-Turkish War population exchange, and was itself renamed from the functional Vromeroskala.

cultural_refs.title: EU Blue Flag certification
cultural_refs.description: The Blue Flag is a European eco-certification for beaches and marinas; Olympiaki Akti has held it every year except 1998.

recurring_events.name: Feast of Agios Prokopios
recurring_events.description: The name day of Saint Prokopios, patron of the settlement's parish church, falls on 8 July in the Orthodox liturgical calendar — the closest thing Olympic Beach has to a fixed annual local observance.

things_to_know.label: The population is disputed
things_to_know.note: The 2021 census is cited as 236 residents by English Wikipedia and 420 by Greek Wikipedia for the same settlement; neither source links a resolving primary document.

things_to_know.label: Airport distance depends on how you measure it
things_to_know.note: Thessaloniki International Airport (SKG) is 45 km away in a straight line, but the drive around the Thermaic Gulf via the A1/E75 motorway is roughly 107 km, per Wikipedia's infobox distance.

things_to_know.label: Mount Olympus is visible, not adjacent
things_to_know.note: The mountain the beach is named for sits about 26 km southwest in a straight line; it is a horizon feature on clear days, not a backdrop you walk to from the sand.

things_to_know.label: One missing Blue Flag year
things_to_know.note: The beach has held the EU Blue Flag every year except 1998; no source used for this page explains the gap.

access_note: Olympic Beach (Olympiaki Akti) sits about 7.5 km southeast of Katerini's city center and roughly 3 km south of Paralia, reached via the A1/E75 motorway's Katerini South interchange, which links directly to the settlement. Katerini's railway station, 7.1 km away, serves Proastiakos suburban trains and the Athens–Thessaloniki InterCity line. Thessaloniki International Airport (SKG) is 45 km away by straight line but about 107 km by road around the gulf, roughly 1.5 hours' drive.
